name: Vetiver Green
lede: Vetiver Green is a dusty, grey-tinged olive, named for the fragrant tropical grass whose roots are used in perfume and thatch, first plated by Ridgway in 1912.

sections.title: A grass root's grey-green
sections.body:
Robert Ridgway recorded this hue in 1912, plate XLVII, hue 25'''', and both the ISCC-NBS block list of 1955 and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary carry it on from there [1]. Vetiver is a perennial grass grown for its roots, which are distilled into a smoky, earthy perfume oil rather than for any green part of the plant, so the name borrows the plant's identity, not a leaf or root color actually matched to it [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[silver-green]], [[artichoke-green]], [[eucalyptus]] and [[celadon-green]], at 2.8, 2.8, [[eucalyptus]] sits only slightly further off, duller and greyer again [2]. Measured in LCH it is lightness 62, chroma 21, hue 109 degrees, a muted yellow-green with little saturation [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this olive in 1,173 of 23,781 paintings (4.93%, as photographed), more common than 86% of the named colors we track [3]. It most often plays a light within a painting, in 35% of its 660 strongest matches [3]. Christen Købke is its most devoted painter, appearing in 6 of his 50 works at 4.0 times the baseline rate [3]. The earliest dated match runs back to 916, nearly a thousand years before the name itself was recorded in 1912; the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that the pigment was there, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].
